title: Python Day 7: Positional-Only, Keyword-Only Arguments and Return Statement
author: Vasanthakumari N
summary: 1. Positional-Only Arguments (/) In Python, / is used as a positional-only argument separator. It means that the parameters written before / must be passed using their position. We cannot pass them using parameter names (keyword arguments). Example: def calculate ( a , b , / ) : print ( a + b ) calculate ( 10 , 20 ) # 30 calculate ( a = 10 , b = 20 ) # TypeError TypeError: calculate() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments Here, a and b must be passed as positional arguments. 2. Keyword-Only Arguments (*) In Python, * can be used as a keyword-only argument separator. It means that the parameters written after * must be passed using their parameter names. Example: def calculate ( a , * , b ) : print ( a + b ) calculate ( a = 10 , b = 20 ) # 30 calculate ( 10 , b = 20 ) # 30 calculate ( 10 , 20 ) # Error TypeError: calculate() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given Here: a can be passed as either a positional or keyword argument. b must be passed as a keyword argument. Difference Between / and * Symbol Meaning / Parameters before it are positional-only * Parameters after it are keyword-only Remember: / separates positional-only parameters. * separates keyword-only parameters. Return Statement in Python The return statement is used to send a value from a function back to the place where the function was called. Example: def play ( ) : teamA = 300 teamB = 290 if teamA > teamB : return "Winner Trophy" else : return "Runner Trophy" hand = play ( ) print ( hand ) Output: Winner Trophy

title: Fixing PyInstaller --onefile tmpfs Issues by Switching to --onedir and Clarifying Size Myths
author: Roman Dubrovin
summary: Anatomy of the --onefile vs. --onedir Bundle and the Size Myth When you pass --onefile to PyInstaller, the build tool does not strip dead code, prune unused shared libraries, or shrink your Python interpreter. Instead, the bootloader appends a compressed archive (typically using zlib or LZMA) containing the exact same set of .pyc bytecode files, .so / .dll shared objects, and data assets that a --onedir build places into a directory tree. If your bundle contains a 600 MB scientific or machine learning stack, --onefile still carries all 600 MB of underlying payload inside that single executable. Any file-size reduction you observe on disk comes from archive compression ratios minus a small bootloader stub, whereas at runtime the uncompressed bytes must be written out anyway—meaning --onefile often inflates temporary storage pressure rather than saving space. The physical cause of tmpfs failures lies in how a --onefile binary boots. When launched, the C bootloader reads the embedded archive, decompresses each entry, and writes the unpacked files into a temporary directory—commonly under /tmp or TMPDIR —before loading the embedded Python runtime from those extracted files. Because tmpfs stores files in page cache backed by system RAM and swap rather than a persistent block device, every decompressed byte occupies volatile memory pages or hits a strict tmpfs size cap (such as a container's default 64 MB /dev/shm or tight /tmp mount). As decompressed bytes accumulate in tmpfs , free memory pages shrink or the mount hits its quota; once exhausted, the write syscall fails with ENOSPC (no space left on device) or the kernel's out-of-memory (OOM) killer terminates the process. Startup latency follows a parallel mechanical chain. Under --onefile , cold start requires sequential decompression and filesystem writes of potentially hundreds of megabytes into the temporary directory on every invocation, followed by dynamic linker symbol resolution and Python imports. Under --onedir , the files already sit unpacked on disk or in an existing directory, so launching skips the full-bundle decompression-and-extraction pass and goes straight to loading shared libraries and executing Python code. However, --onedir is not universally faster: if a network filesystem has high metadata latency across thousands of small files, or if a warm tmpfs page cache already holds the extracted payload while cold storage is slow, those local I/O dynamics can shift the balance. Decision Dominance: Choosing Between --onedir and --onefile Optimal default for tmpfs-constrained and production runtimes: --onedir . By eliminating runtime self-extraction into volatile temporary storage, --onedir avoids ENOSPC quota exhaustion and avoids duplicating payload bytes across both archive/page cache and extracted files in RAM-backed tmpfs . It is strictly more reliable than --onefile when temporary space is bounded or memory is tight. When --onedir stops working: When the deployment target only permits distributing a single standalone binary file with no directory bundle or archive wrapper allowed, or when the target filesystem has severe per-file open/stat overhead across thousands of tiny dependency files and cannot be pre-staged. Typical choice errors and their mechanism: Engineers frequently pick --onefile assuming single-file packaging shrinks the application, when in reality compression only trades CPU decompression time for a smaller transfer artifact while expanding back to full size in tmpfs at runtime. Another common mistake is pointing TMPDIR at a larger tmpfs mount without checking total system RAM: expanding tmpfs capacity without sufficient backing RAM/swap simply allows a giant extraction to push the host closer to OOM eviction. Selection rule: If /tmp or TMPDIR is backed by memory-capped tmpfs , or if cold-start speed and predictable memory headroom matter more than a single-file artifact -> use --onedir . Only use --onefile when a single-file executable is a hard distribution requirement and the target environment has ample temporary storage and RAM headroom to absorb full decompression on every launch. Why --onefile Breaks on tmpfs: Extraction, Memory, and Execution Constraints When a PyInstaller --onefile executable launches, a compiled C bootloader opens its own binary image, locates the trailing archive appended during build, decompresses entries (typically zlib or LZMA), and writes every extracted file into a temporary directory under TMPDIR or /tmp before starting the embedded Python runtime. When that target directory sits on a tmpfs mount, those writes do not hit a disk block layer; they allocate kernel page cache backed by physical RAM and swap. Switching to --onedir eliminates this runtime extraction phase because the bootloader loads pre-unpacked .pyc bytecode, shared libraries, and data files directly from disk rather than materializing a second copy in volatile memory. A common assumption is that --onefile shrinks an application because it produces a single file. It does not prune unused modules, strip dead bytecode, or shrink shared libraries; it packages the same dependency graph as --onedir inside a compressed container plus a bootloader stub. Any file-size reduction comes strictly from archive compression minus bootloader overhead, while runtime execution still inflates the uncompressed payload. Core Failure Mechanics on tmpfs Mount cap exhaustion (ENOSPC): Each extracted file written to a size-capped tmpfs mount consumes filesystem blocks out of the mount's configured capacity limit. Once uncompressed bytes plus filesystem metadata exceed that cap, the kernel rejects further write syscalls with ENOSPC , aborting bootloader extraction before Python starts. Page-cache and RAM pressure (OOM killer): Because tmpfs stores file contents in memory pages rather than persistent blocks, extracting a large scientific or AI bundle expands anonymous/page-cache memory usage while the Python process simultaneously allocates heap for interpreters and loaded .so libraries. When total memory and swap demand crosses the cgroup or system limit, the kernel out-of-memory (OOM) killer terminates the process. Noexec and permission enforcement: Bootloaders unpack shared libraries and helper binaries into the temp directory and invoke dynamic linking or execution against those extracted paths. If the tmpfs mount carries noexec or restricted permissions, loading shared objects or executing extracted binaries fails at the kernel/loader boundary even when free space and RAM remain available. Cold-start extraction latency: Every cold launch of a --onefile binary repeats archive scanning, decompression CPU work, and temp-directory file creation before symbol resolution and module imports even begin. A --onedir build bypasses decompression and write amplification on launch, moving straight to opening existing files. Five Deployment Scenarios Where --onefile Fails Deployment Scenario Physical Constraint Causal Failure Chain Observable Effect Restricted container /tmp Capped tmpfs on /tmp with tight container memory limit Bootloader decompresses bundle into /tmp -> page cache fills capped tmpfs or pushes cgroup memory to limit -> write returns ENOSPC or cgroup OOM kills task Immediate startup crash with extraction write error or silent exit code 137 Shared-memory /tmp mapped to /dev/shm /tmp symlinked or bound to small /dev/shm segment Unpacked shared libraries and data exceed small shared-memory cap -> page allocation hits segment ceiling -> archive unpack halts mid-stream Partial temp folder and failed PyInstaller bootloader extraction error Hardened Linux runtime with noexec /tmp tmpfs mounted with noexec (and sometimes nosuid / nodev ) Bootloader writes .so or binary payloads to /tmp -> dlopen or execve hits noexec mount flag -> kernel blocks code execution Dynamic linker or permission/execution failure during runtime initialization High-concurrency worker autoscaling Multiple --onefile workers starting simultaneously on one host Concurrent processes decompress duplicate bundles into tmpfs -> multiplied page-cache footprint and CPU decompression contention -> memory exhausts host RAM/swap Cascading OOM kills and multi-second startup spikes across workers Low-RAM embedded or edge Linux node Limited physical RAM with little or no swap Decompressed payload plus Python/ML runtime heap exceeds physical page frames -> memory reclaim cannot free pinned/active pages -> kernel OOM killer triggers Process killed mid-import or right after extraction completes --onedir vs. --onefile: Effectiveness and Edge Cases --onedir is the optimal default for server, container, and edge deployments. By keeping files unpacked in a directory, it removes per-launch decompression work, avoids duplicate byte materialization inside tmpfs , and makes memory consumption much more predictable. It also matches actual on-disk payload reality: a 600 MB scientific or AI stack is roughly 600 MB of actual code, libraries, and data either way, so --onefile is trading startup time and runtime memory/temp overhead for single-file convenience rather than shrinking the real application footprint. Even --onedir stops working cleanly under specific edge conditions. If a distribution pipeline strictly mandates a single standalone binary with zero supporting directories or wrapper scripts, --onedir does not meet that packaging constraint. In addition, when a --onedir bundle containing thousands of small files sits on a high-metadata-latency network filesystem without pre-staging, repeated open and stat round-trips across many tiny files can slow startup, whereas a warm tmpfs page cache or slow cold storage can invert relative I/O costs between the two modes. Typical Choice Errors and Selection Rule Treating --onefile as a footprint shrinker: Teams often pick --onefile expecting a smaller app, overlooking that archive compression only packs the same underlying dependencies on disk while unpacking them back into memory or temp storage at runtime. Raising tmpfs size without RAM/swap headroom: Increasing a tmpfs TMPDIR limit lets extraction write more bytes into page cache, which removes ENOSPC only to push total memory usage past physical RAM and swap into an OOM kill. Pointing TMPDIR at a noexec mount: Redirecting TMPDIR to another tmpfs volume without checking mount flags can still block shared-library loading if noexec is set. Decision rule: If /tmp or TMPDIR is backed by a memory-capped tmpfs , or if cold-start speed and predictable RAM headroom matter more than a single file, use --onedir ; use --onefile only when a hard single-file requirement applies and temp storage plus RAM/swap have enough headroom for full per-launch extraction. Fixing PyInstaller --onefile tmpfs Issues by Switching to --onedir and Clarifying Size Myths When a Python service or CLI tool built with PyInstaller --onefile starts failing inside containers, restricted Linux pods, or low-memory nodes, the culprit is almost always how the bootloader handles temporary storage on tmpfs . Switching from --onefile to --onedir is the right fix in most server and container environments. It eliminates per-launch extraction onto memory-backed temporary filesystems, cuts cold-start overhead, and preserves predictable memory headroom without actually costing you real-world application size. A common misconception is that --onefile shrinks your application. It does not prune unused imports, strip dead bytecode, or drop shared libraries from your dependency graph. It takes the exact same set of .pyc files, .so or .dll shared objects, and data files that --onedir places into a folder, compresses them into a trailing archive (typically zlib or LZMA), and attaches a C bootloader stub. If your scientific or AI stack unpacks to 600 MB, all 600 MB of underlying code and libraries still exist inside the single binary. The single executable looks smaller on disk only because the archive is compressed minus the bootloader stub's bytes; the moment it runs, those compressed bytes must be decompressed and written back out in uncompressed form. Why --onefile Breaks on tmpfs Unlike a persistent block device such as an ext4 or XFS disk partition, tmpfs stores files in volatile page cache backed by physical RAM and swap. When a --onefile binary launches, its C bootloader reads its own trailing archive, decompresses entries in sequence, and writes the unpacked files into a temporary directory under TMPDIR or /tmp before starting the embedded Python runtime. Mount cap exhaustion (ENOSPC): Writing uncompressed shared libraries and assets into a size-capped tmpfs mount allocates page cache entries against that mount limit. Once the unpacked payload plus filesystem metadata hits the cap, the kernel rejects subsequent write syscalls with ENOSPC , aborting startup before Python imports even begin. RAM and swap pressure (OOM killer): Every byte written to tmpfs consumes memory pages alongside the Python interpreter heap, NumPy or PyTorch allocations, and mapped shared libraries. When combined page cache and process memory cross a cgroup limit or host RAM-plus-swap capacity, memory reclaim cannot free enough clean pages fast enough, and the Linux OOM killer terminates the process (often surfacing as exit code 137). Hardened mount permissions (noexec): Security-hardened containers frequently mount /tmp or TMPDIR with noexec (often paired with nosuid and nodev ). Even when free space and RAM are plentiful, extracting .so libraries or helper binaries into a noexec mount causes dynamic linking ( dlopen ) or execution ( execve ) to fail with permission errors because the kernel blocks code execution from that mount. Concurrent worker spikes: Scaling out multiple --onefile workers on one host triggers simultaneous archive decompression and page-cache growth across processes, compounding CPU load and pushing shared RAM/swap into contention or OOM kills. Comparative Trade-Offs: Reliability, Startup Latency, and Operational Overhead Choosing between --onedir and --onefile is an operational trade-off between single-artifact convenience and runtime determinism. Once unpacked, both modes load shared objects and execute Python bytecode in the same general runtime model, but --onefile pays an extraction tax on every cold start while competing for tmpfs memory. Containerization and memory predictability: In Docker or Kubernetes, --onedir copies a pre-unpacked directory into the container image layer once at build time. At runtime, shared libraries and data files are read straight from the container filesystem rather than duplicated into a memory-capped tmpfs /tmp or /dev/shm . That keeps memory usage much more predictable under tight cgroup limits. CI/CD and artifact distribution: --onefile wins on raw distribution simplicity when you must ship a single standalone file over a basic upload step, copy it to an air-gapped target, or hand a single binary to users without packaging a tarball or zip archive. --onedir requires archiving and unpacking a directory (such as a .tar.gz ) in your build and deploy pipeline, adding a small packaging step in CI/CD so runtime hosts do not have to unpack on every launch. Filesystem permissions and hardening: Because --onedir lives in a known application directory (for example, /opt/app ) rather than extracting executables into /tmp at runtime, it avoids noexec failures on /tmp and makes file ownership and read/execute permissions explicit at deploy time. Cold-start speed: Every --onefile cold launch must scan the archive, run decompression CPU cycles, and create temporary files before Python starts importing modules. --onedir skips full-bundle extraction and goes straight to opening existing files and resolving symbols, making cold starts faster in standard local and container setups. Edge Cases and Failure Modes of --onedir --onedir is not immune to environmental bottlenecks. If you place a large --onedir bundle containing thousands of small .pyc and dependency files onto a high-metadata-latency network filesystem (such as certain remote NFS or shared mounts) without pre-staging locally, repeated open and stat calls during Python startup can introduce noticeable latency—sometimes enough to invert the usual startup advantage over a warm tmpfs cache. It also falls short whenever a distribution policy strictly forbids a directory bundle or wrapper script. Engineers running into --onefile tmpfs errors frequently make three mechanical mistakes: treating --onefile as if it shrinks runtime memory or dependency size; enlarging a tmpfs TMPDIR limit without adding backing RAM or swap (which simply shifts failures from ENOSPC to OOM kills); or pointing TMPDIR to another tmpfs path without checking whether noexec is set. Decision Rule If /tmp or TMPDIR sits on a memory-capped tmpfs, or if cold-start speed and predictable RAM headroom matter more than shipping a single file, use --onedir. Use --onefile only when a strict single-file requirement applies and the target host has enough temporary storage, non-noexec permissions, and RAM/swap headroom to absorb full decompression on every launch. Why --onedir Beats --onefile on tmpfs and What --onefile Actually Shrinks When a PyInstaller --onefile binary fails on tmpfs , the failure is not a quirk of PyInstaller being picky about temporary folders—it is a resource collision between archive decompression and memory-backed filesystem allocation. Switching to --onedir is the right move for servers, containers, and edge runtimes because it eliminates per-launch self-extraction, keeps memory consumption predictable, and exposes the true uncompressed size of your application rather than hiding it behind a zip or LZMA wrapper. A common myth is that --onefile shrinks the application. It does not prune unused imports, strip dead bytecode, or drop heavy scientific or AI libraries from the dependency graph. It packs the exact same .pyc files, shared libraries ( .so or .dll ), and data assets into a compressed archive appended to a C bootloader stub. On disk, the single binary looks smaller only because archive compression (such as zlib or LZMA) squeezes repetitive bytes minus the bootloader overhead. At runtime, the bootloader still decompresses that payload and writes the full unpacked tree to disk before embedded Python starts. A 600 MB scientific or numerical stack is still 600 MB of code and libraries once materialized. How --onefile Breaks tmpfs and Inflates Startup Latency Unlike a persistent block device such as ext4 or XFS , tmpfs stores files in volatile kernel page cache backed by physical RAM and swap. When a --onefile process launches, its C bootloader reads the trailing archive, decompresses entries sequentially, and issues write syscalls into TMPDIR (often /tmp ) before Python imports begin. Each causal failure chain traces directly to that extraction step: Mount cap exhaustion (ENOSPC): Sequential decompression writes uncompressed files plus filesystem metadata into tmpfs page cache -> allocated pages reach the tmpfs size cap -> subsequent write syscalls fail with ENOSPC -> startup aborts before Python initializes. RAM and swap pressure (OOM killer, exit code 137): Decompressed tmpfs pages expand concurrently with the Python heap, numerical or ML array allocations, and mapped shared libraries -> total anonymous and page-cache memory crosses the cgroup or host RAM-plus-swap ceiling faster than page reclaim can free clean or movable pages -> the Linux OOM killer terminates the process with exit code 137 . Hardened mount enforcement (noexec): Security-hardened hosts mount /tmp or TMPDIR with noexec (often alongside nosuid and nodev ) -> the bootloader extracts .so libraries or helper binaries into that directory, then calls dlopen or execve -> the kernel blocks execution on the noexec mount despite free space and free RAM -> dynamic linking or binary launch fails immediately. Concurrent worker spikes: Multiple --onefile workers start on the same host simultaneously -> parallel decompression multiplies CPU load while multiple tmpfs directories expand page cache at once -> host memory pressure spikes and triggers cascading OOM kills or multi-second startup stalls. Cold-start overhead: Every cold launch repeats archive scanning, decompression CPU cycles, and temp-file creation before module imports even start, whereas --onedir opens pre-extracted files directly. Decision Framework and Migration Checklist for Moving to --onedir Between the two modes, --onedir is the superior default whenever you control the runtime environment, care about cold-start speed, or run inside memory-constrained containers and edge nodes. It places pre-unpacked files in an explicit directory (such as /opt/app ) with deterministic ownership and permissions, avoiding tmpfs bloat and /tmp noexec traps. --onedir stops working cleanly under two clear conditions: first, when distribution policy or packaging rules strictly require a single standalone executable with no supporting directory or wrapper; second, when a bundle containing thousands of small files is placed directly on a high-latency network filesystem (such as remote NFS) without local staging, where thousands of open and stat round-trips can make startup slower than unpacking into a warm local cache. Engineers frequently make three avoidable mistakes when troubleshooting --onefile tmpfs failures. First, they assume --onefile reduces runtime RAM or trims unused dependencies, ignoring that unpacked artifacts still enter memory or page cache. Second, they enlarge the tmpfs size cap without adding backing RAM or swap, which merely trades an ENOSPC write error for an OOM kill when memory fills. Third, they point TMPDIR at another tmpfs mount without checking whether noexec is set, leaving dlopen and execve blocked. Selection rule: If /tmp or TMPDIR sits on a memory-capped tmpfs , or if cold-start latency, predictable cgroup memory headroom, and explicit file permissions matter most, use --onedir . Use --onefile only when a strict single-file requirement applies and the target host provides enough temporary storage, non- noexec permissions, and RAM-plus-swap headroom for full decompression on every launch. If --onefile must stay in place temporarily, contain the blast radius by setting TMPDIR to a non- noexec persistent or local scratch path with verified free space, sizing RAM and swap above peak unpacked payload plus runtime heap, and staging concurrent worker starts rather than launching dozens in lockstep. Switch the build spec to --onedir: Update your PyInstaller build command or .spec file from --onefile to --onedir and inspect the actual uncompressed directory size and largest dependencies. Package and transfer as an archive: Bundle the output directory (for example, with tar.gz ) in CI/CD so artifacts move cleanly between build stages, registries, or release hosts. Install into a non-tmpfs directory with explicit permissions: Extract the bundle into a persistent path such as /opt/app (or bake it into the container image layer at build time) with explicit read/execute permissions and ownership rather than relying on /tmp . Avoid high-latency network mounts for raw --onedir trees: If deploying to network storage, copy or unpack onto local disk or container storage before execution rather than serving thousands of small files over a high-latency share. Verify cold-start latency and cgroup memory under concurrency: Benchmark startup time and peak RSS/cgroup memory with realistic worker concurrency, confirming tmpfs usage stays flat and exit code 137 OOM kills disappear.

title: When you replace a library, you also take over everything it did
author: Alkhatib Adam
summary: DPOLens is an open-source MCP server that gives AI assistants the text of privacy law. Its search runs on the CPU, so it needs no GPU. The usual way to run an embedding model in Python is sentence-transformers . DPOLens doesn't use it: with PyTorch's CPU build it installs about 1 GB, against about 200 MB for ONNX Runtime , the tokenizers library and NumPy. So DPOLens calls the model through ONNX Runtime directly, and does the tokenising and pooling itself, in about forty lines. Those forty lines did their job. What they didn't do was what the library does without being asked. When a new instance starts for the first time, it embeds every clause of the law it carries , and while load-testing the community version , I found that this was the heaviest thing DPOLens ever did. In a container limited to 1.5 CPUs, about what a small server offers, it took nearly 23 minutes and peaked at 3.4 GB. Two fixes made it 5.1× faster with 65% less memory, and the vectors came out the same. If you've swapped sentence-transformers for raw ONNX Runtime to slim an image, you probably have both problems too. The setup DPOLens's meaning search uses multilingual-e5-small . A new instance embeds GDPR , the UAE's data protection law and a sample company policy : 1,350 clauses, from 19 to 512 tokens long, 63 in the middle. The vectors go into Postgres with pgvector , so this happens once, before the instance answers anything. Every run below embedded those 1,350 clauses inside the published DPOLens 0.1.0 image, the release before the fixes, from a fresh copy of the same database, with 4 GB of memory and a Docker CPU limit : 1.5 CPUs, 2.5 (what the community version gives this step), or none, which on my laptop is 10 cores. What the library was doing: sorting by length A model reads a batch as one rectangle. Every string is padded to the longest in its batch, and the padding costs as much work as the text. sentence-transformers sorts its inputs by length before it batches them, so each batch holds strings of about one length. My forty lines didn't. They embedded 64 clauses at a time in the order they're stored, so a 20-token paragraph next to a 512-token article was read as 512 tokens. I counted: the clauses hold 110,000 real tokens, and the model read 304,000. Almost two thirds of its work was padding. Padding costs memory too, and more than its share: the memory for attention grows with the number of strings in a batch times the square of the longest. A batch of 64 strings at 512 tokens was the heaviest shape 0.1.0 could make, and in stored order, every batch with one long article had that shape. Sorting alone doesn't prevent it, since the library still batches by count, so the fix also caps each batch by that measure, in the spirit of --max-batch-tokens in Hugging Face's Text Embeddings Inference : # How much one batch may hold, as its clauses times the square of the longest, # which is how the memory for attention grows: 64 clauses of 64 tokens, 16 of # 128, or one of 512. BATCH_BUDGET = 64 * 64 * 64 def batches ( tokens : Sequence [ int ] ) -> list [ list [ int ] ] : found : list [ list [ int ] ] = [ ] batch : list [ int ] = [ ] for at in sorted ( range ( len ( tokens ) ) , key = lambda position : tokens [ position ] ) : # Sorted, so this string is the longest the batch would hold. if batch and ( len ( batch ) + 1 ) * tokens [ at ] ** 2 > BATCH_BUDGET : found . append ( batch ) batch = [ ] batch . append ( at ) if batch : found . append ( batch ) return found Sorted and capped, the model reads 114,000 tokens instead of 304,000, and the longest clauses go one at a time. Budgets from half this one to eight times it were no better. What nobody was doing: reading the CPU limit The second problem isn't the library's. Inside a container limited to 2.5 CPUs on a 10-core machine, Python's os.cpu_count() says 10, and ONNX Runtime, left to choose , starts a thread for each of them. A Docker CPU limit isn't a set of cores but a share of time, so ten threads took turns on two and a half CPUs' worth of it. dpolens index build now reads the limit from /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max and rounds it up, so 2.5 CPUs get three threads. With no limit, it takes os.process_cpu_count() , which follows CPU affinity but not a time limit. Picking a fixed number doesn't work: three threads were the best with 2.5 CPUs, and with no limit they took 143 seconds, slower than 0.1.0's 129 with all ten. The results With 2.5 CPUs, each fix on its own, then both: Change Seconds Peak memory 0.1.0 632 3,486 MiB Threads 468 3,488 MiB Sorted 257 1,427 MiB Both 174 1,426 MiB As shipped 163 1,213 MiB The two sorted rows in the middle used a budget four times the one that shipped. Threads changed the time and nothing else. Sorting changed both. Then 0.2.0, which shipped both, against 0.1.0 at each limit: CPU limit Before After Faster 1.5 CPUs 1,375 s 267 s 5.1× 2.5 CPUs 632 s 163 s 3.9× None 129 s 53 s 2.4× The gain is largest where the machine is smallest, which is where a 23-minute first start gets noticed. The peak after, 1,213 MiB at every limit, is exactly what loading the model takes before embedding anything: embedding the whole law now adds nothing measurable to it. Same vectors, same search Padding is masked, so in theory it changes nothing. I checked anyway. 885 of the 1,350 vectors were bit-identical to 0.1.0's, and the rest differed by at most 0.00000011 in any component, the rounding of a batch with a different shape. Every published evaluation set scored the same recall@5, recall@10 and MRR, and a test now checks that each clause's stored vector is the one it gets embedded alone. One more: memory that wasn't given back Measuring the first start also caught DPOLens's worker, which embeds an organisation's policies , loading its own copy of the model for jobs with nothing left to embed, and keeping it. Closing the model wasn't enough either: glibc keeps freed memory for the process, so a process that held 875 MiB with the model loaded still held 440 after closing it, and 93 after malloc_trim(0) . The worker now loads the model only when there's work, and gives the memory back after. It doesn't change what an instance needs , but it frees about 900 MB between jobs. What I took from it A library is more than its API. Forty lines replaced sentence-transformers and kept the image about 800 MB smaller, and they also dropped the sorting the library does without saying so. Sort before you batch, then cap by shape. A batch's memory grows with its strings times the square of the longest, so that's what to limit. A container's CPU limit isn't its core count. os.cpu_count() and ONNX Runtime both see the whole machine. Read /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max , and don't hard-code a number instead. Check the vectors, not only the clock. The same search results are the only reason the change could ship. Everything here was measured on one laptop, with one model, over clauses whose lengths vary a lot: text of one length would gain little from sorting, and your seconds will differ. The batching is in index.py , the thread count in encode.py , and every measurement, including the options I didn't take, in #68 . Both fixes shipped in DPOLens 0.2.0 . To run an instance yourself, start with Get started . DPOLens is open source , under the Apache License 2.0. First published on dpolens.com . DPOLens is an open-source MCP server that gives AI assistants privacy law and an organisation's own policies, clause by clause: github.com/alkhatibdev/dpolens .

title: Cropping 101 photos into two screens without losing the subject
author: 尚毅段
summary: Cropping 101 photos into two screens without losing the subject The iPhone Duo has two displays that don't share an aspect ratio. The inner screen is landscape, 2670x1878. The cover screen is portrait, 1398x2034. A wallpaper that looks right on one is usually wrong on the other, so every image on Best iPhone Duo ships as two separate crops plus a 4K version. Doing that with Image.thumbnail() produced 101 wallpapers I didn't want to look at. Centre cropping a landscape photo to 1398x2034 keeps the middle strip and throws away the edges, which on a mountain lake means the horizon sits dead centre and the far ridge disappears. So the build does the crop decision itself. What the crop has to decide For each source image, three targets. The inner screen gets 2670x1878, the 4K download gets 3840x2700, and the cover screen gets 1398x2034. Two are landscape, one is portrait, all from the same photograph. The rule I wanted: keep the part of the image with the most detail, but don't drift so far that the frame looks accidental. Edge density is a decent proxy for "the interesting part" on landscape photos — a treeline, a skyline, a ridge. Edge energy as a crop guide Downscale to 320px wide, convert to greyscale, run an edge filter, then sum edge pixels into a 1D profile along the axis being cropped: def energy_profile ( im , axis ) : g = im . convert ( "L" ) . resize ( ( 320 , max ( 1 , int ( 320 * im . height / im . width ) ) ) , Image . LANCZOS ) e = g . filter ( ImageFilter . FIND_EDGES ) w , h = e . size px = list ( e . getdata ( ) ) if axis == 0 : return [ sum ( px [ y * w + x ] for y in range ( 0 , h , 2 ) ) for x in range ( w ) ] return [ sum ( px [ y * w + x ] for x in range ( 0 , w , 2 ) ) for y in range ( h ) ] That gives you a column profile for horizontal crops and a row profile for vertical ones. Then slide a window the width of the crop across the profile and take the one with the most energy: def pick_offset ( prof , span , total , prefer = 0.5 ) : n = len ( prof ) if span >= n : return 0 win = min ( int ( n * span / total ) or 1 , n - 1 ) best , best_i = - 1 , 0 step = max ( 1 , win // 12 ) for i in range ( 0 , n - win + 1 , step ) : s = sum ( prof [ i : i + win ] ) centre = ( i + win / 2 ) / n s *= ( 1 - 0.25 * abs ( centre - prefer ) * 2 ) if s > best : best , best_i = s , i return int ( best_i / n * total ) The prefer term is the part that matters. Pure max-energy cropping chases a bright sky or a busy foreground and produces frames where the subject is jammed against one edge. Multiplying the score by a penalty on distance from a target centre pulls it back. For the inner screen that target is 0.5, dead centre. For the cover screen it's 0.42, slightly toward the top. That number came from trying a handful of crops and keeping what looked right; there is no data behind it. Two constants, and the crops stopped looking accidental. Output sizes Each photo becomes five files: File Size Used for -open.jpg 2670x1878 inner screen download -cover.jpg 1398x2034 cover screen download -4k.jpg 3840x2700 4K download -open-thumb.jpg 960x675 grid preview -cover-thumb.jpg 420x611 cover preview JPEG throughout, quality 80 for the inner screen, 82 for the cover, 72 for 4K, progressive and optimised. 101 photographs come to 277MB total, which only works because each file is served immutable for a year and the grid only ever loads the thumbnails. The accent colour for each card comes from the same resized image — a 24x24 average, no extra pass over the full-size file. What this doesn't do It's not a face-aware crop. On a photo where the subject is small and off-centre, edge energy can prefer a detailed background over the person. The offsets also aren't stored per image: every wallpaper uses the same two prefer values, so a crop that comes out wrong has to be fixed by replacing the source photo, not by nudging a field in the build. The photos themselves are Creative Commons from Wikimedia Commons, mostly CC BY 4.0, credited to the photographer on each wallpaper page. The gallery is at bestiphoneduo.com if you want to see how the two crops sit next to each other.

title: Raspberry Pi 5 vs Orange Pi 5 vs NVIDIA Jetson (2026 Guide)
author: guang diyuzhi
summary: Why Developers Care About SBCs in 2026 Single-board computers have evolved far beyond Arduino projects. With the Raspberry Pi 5 offering desktop-class performance, the Orange Pi 5 delivering 8-core ARM power, and the NVIDIA Jetson bringing GPU acceleration, these boards are now viable for real development work — from home labs to edge AI. The SBC market in 2026 offers more choice than ever, but each board targets a distinctly different developer profile. Choosing the wrong one means either overpaying for hardware you never use or hitting a performance ceiling months into a project. Quick Verdict Raspberry Pi 5 — Best for beginners, education, and projects that benefit from the largest software ecosystem on the planet. If you want something that "just works" with the most tutorials, forums, and accessory support, this is your board. Score: 8/10.Orange Pi 5 — Best performance-per-dollar in the SBC world. The Rockchip RK3588S delivers desktop-class CPU power, built-in NPU, and native NVMe storage at a price that undercuts the Pi 5 on raw specs. Ideal for home servers and developers comfortable with Armbian. Score: 9/10.NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano — The only choice when your project needs real GPU compute. 40 TOPS of AI performance, full CUDA support, and NVIDIA's mature SDK ecosystem make it the default for robotics, computer vision, and edge inference. Overkill for basic projects. Score: 8/10. Hardware Specs Comparison Specification Raspberry Pi 5 Orange Pi 5 NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano SoC Broadcom BCM2712 Rockchip RK3588S NVIDIA Orin (ARM v8.2) CPU Cores 4× Cortex-A76 @ 2.4 GHz 4× A76 + 4× A55 @ 2.4/1.8 GHz 6× Cortex-A78AE @ 1.5 GHz GPU VideoCore VII Mali-G610 MP4 1024 CUDA + 32 Tensor Cores RAM 4 / 8 GB LPDDR4X 4 / 8 / 16 GB LPDDR4X 4 / 8 GB LPDDR5 AI Acceleration None 6 TOPS NPU 40 TOPS Storage microSD, PCIe 2.0 x1 (via HAT) NVMe M.2 PCIe 3.0 x2 (native) M.2 Key M NVMe Video Output 2× HDMI 4K@60 1× HDMI 2.1 8K, 1× HDMI 2.0 1× HDMI 2.0 4K@60 Networking Gigabit, WiFi 5, BT 5.0 Gigabit, WiFi 6, BT 5.0 Gigabit (no WiFi included) GPIO 40-pin standard 26-pin (partially compatible) Carrier-specific headers Power 5V / 5A USB-C 5V / 4A USB-C 7–20V DC barrel Price $60 (4GB) / $80 (8GB) $69 (4GB) / $99 (8GB) / $149 (16GB) $199 (4GB) / $299 (8GB) Performance Benchmarks CPU Multicore: Orange Pi 5 wins decisively — eight physical cores versus four on the Pi 5 and six lower-clock cores on the Jetson. For compilation, Docker workloads, and parallel tasks, it is the clear leader. GPU / AI: Jetson destroys both — 1024 CUDA cores + 32 Tensor cores (40 TOPS) handle real-time object detection, LLM inference, and video processing that neither ARM board can touch. The Orange Pi 5's 6 TOPS NPU is useful for lightweight inference, while the Pi 5 has no hardware AI acceleration at all. General Development: Raspberry Pi 5 feels smoothest for everyday use thanks to Raspberry Pi OS's mature optimization and hardware-accelerated desktop compositing. Orange Pi 5's raw horsepower is noticeable in compilation, but Armbian's desktop is less polished. Storage Speed: Orange Pi 5 with native NVMe delivers sequential reads exceeding 3,500 MB/s — roughly 5–6× faster than the Pi 5's microSD and 2–3× faster than the Pi 5 even with a PCIe NVMe HAT (limited to PCIe 2.0 x1). Use Case Recommendations 🏠 Home Lab & Self-Hosting Pick: Orange Pi 5 — The 16 GB RAM + native NVMe makes this an excellent low-power server for Docker, Coolify, or Kubernetes. Three times more RAM per dollar than the Pi 5, and eight cores handle concurrent containers effortlessly. See our Coolify vs Dokku vs CapRover comparison for deployment options. 🎓 Learning & Education Pick: Raspberry Pi 5 — The ecosystem is overwhelming: hundreds of tutorials, first-party curriculum, broadest accessory compatibility (HATs, cameras, displays), and a polished desktop. For teaching or school labs, this is the only choice. 🤖 Edge AI, Robotics & Computer Vision Pick: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano — For YOLO detection, pose estimation, autonomous navigation, or quantized LLMs at the edge, the Jetson is in a different league. The NVIDIA SDK — JetPack, DeepStream, Isaac ROS — provides production tooling ARM SBCs cannot match. The Orange Pi 5's 6 TOPS NPU is a budget alternative for lightweight always-on CV. 🔌 Embedded / IoT Projects Pick: Raspberry Pi 5 — The 40-pin GPIO with decades of community knowledge, HAT compatibility, and programmable I/O via the RP1 chip make the Pi 5 the natural choice for sensor networks and automation. Pros and Cons Raspberry Pi 5 Pros: Best software support, massive community, polished OS, broad accessory ecosystem, reliable and documented, excellent power efficiency. Cons: Only 4 cores, no NPU, microSD bottleneck (NVMe needs a HAT with PCIe 2.0 x1), max 8 GB RAM, WiFi 5 only. Orange Pi 5 Pros: Best CPU performance per dollar, built-in 6 TOPS NPU, native NVMe, up to 16 GB RAM, 8 cores, WiFi 6, HDMI 2.1 8K. Cons: Software support lags behind Pi, Armbian effectively required, 26-pin GPIO only partially Pi-compatible, smaller community, driver issues. NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Pros: Only SBC with CUDA GPU, 40 TOPS AI, excellent NVIDIA SDK (JetPack, DeepStream, Isaac ROS), purpose-built for AI/robotics. Cons: Most expensive, overkill for non-AI, no standard GPIO, limited general-purpose software, higher power, no WiFi/BT. Final Verdict Each SBC serves a distinctly different developer need. The Raspberry Pi 5 is the safest choice — reliable, well-supported, perfect for learning and embedded projects. The Orange Pi 5 offers exceptional value for developers who need raw CPU power, RAM capacity, and fast storage at a low price. The NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano is the specialist's tool, indispensable for GPU-accelerated AI workloads. Category Ratings: Raspberry Pi 5 — 8/10 (reliability + ecosystem). Orange Pi 5 — 9/10 (value + performance). Jetson Orin Nano — 8/10 (AI dominance). Overall: 8/10 Choose based on your project requirements, not benchmark numbers alone. The best SBC is the one that ships your product, not the one that scores highest in Geekbench. Related Articles VS Code vs JetBrains in 2026: Which IDE Should You Actually Use? title: Poki – How Browser Based Games Are Changing Online Gaming
author: Tech Earth Global Business Solution
summary: Have you ever wanted to play a game but didn’t want to have to download any apps or worry about large amounts of data? You’ll probably be looking for something easy to play. This is where sites like Poki come into play. Poki is a website that allows you to play hundreds of games . You can easily find and play new games from various categories. No downloads needed. But How Can You Play games from a website? Thanks to web development technologies, we can. Let’s look at how Poki works and how browser based games show how far technology has come. What Is Poki? Poki is a free website that gives you the opportunity to play games from various developers. You can easily search through a massive amount of games. All you need to do is go to https://poki.com and select a game. What is interesting about this website is that you don’t need a high end gaming system to play the games and most of the games aren’t even downloadable. With this site you can: Search through racing, action, puzzle and adventure games. Play selected multiplayer games. Play on a mobile or desktop browser. Try new games without downloading any apps. Save your progress using account features. Poki will also work with game developers. How Can You Play Games On Poki Without Downloading? This is probably the most interesting part. TTraditional computer games usually require you to download and install their files, while browser-based games load directly in your web browser. Think of it like watching a video online. Your browser doesn’t need to download the entire file before playing it. Similarly, browser games load the required resources through the internet as you play. Typically you’ll: 1.Go to the gaming site and select a game. 2.Your browser will ask for the resources. 3.Resources will load in your browser with supporting code. 4.Resources will process on your device. 5.You can now play! Depending on how developers build the game, the experience may vary. This means that browser based games are super easy to play. You can try out a variety of games without worrying about taking up any space on your device. What Technologies Are Used For Browser Games? Whilst you don’t need to know any coding to play an online game it can be interesting to know how they work. Modern AI technology is also changing how people use digital platforms and online services. Modern browser games use various technologies that web developers will be familiar with. HTML5 An important part of modern web development is HTML5. This allows developers to create interactive pages with media. One useful feature of HTML5 is the Canvas element. This can help with graphics, animations and more. For example, developers can use Canvas to display 2D game visuals, such as racing tracks, cars and other objects in a racing game. JavaScript Games would be pretty boring without interaction. This is where JavaScript can help. JavaScript can help developers create interactive features within the game. For example, if you press a key, click a button or move a character. JavaScript can be Used For: Character movement. Score/timer. Keyboard controls. Animations. Events and rules. This is one reason why modern websites offer so much more. WebGL Have you ever played a 3D game on your browser and wondered how it works without having to download a gaming app? This is where WebGL can help. This allows compatible browsers to display 2D/3D visuals using your device graphics. Developers can create more detailed graphics depending on the game and device. Servers & Internet Something you may not realise is that browser games use servers. When you play a game your browser will ask for some files/resources. Your servers will handle this process. If you play a multiplayer game you may use online infrastructure to communicate with other players. Your browser will give you the environment and the internet will help you with the resources. Note: Developers commonly use these technologies to build browser-based games. Individual games may use different tools. Why Are People Playing Browser Based Games? Not everyone wants to pay for gaming equipment or download large apps. Sometimes people just want to play a quick game. Here are a few reasons why browser based games are popular. No Downloads – No downloads needed. Just open a compatible browser and play! Easy To Access – Easy to find a variety of games. Multiple Devices – Many browser games can be played on computers, smart phones and tablets. This will depend on the game. Quick To Play – Some games can be played in a few minutes. No High End Equipment – Many simple browser games can be played on standard devices. More advanced games may require better equipment. title: PHP's November 2026 Security Release: How to Check, Patch and Restart (and What's New in PHP 8.6)
author: GeekSpark
summary: On November 19, 2026, PHP shipped PHP 8.6.0 and, on the same afternoon, security releases for every supported branch: 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 and 8.2.36 . The security releases fix 17 vulnerabilities , seven rated critical. PHP says the critical ones need non-default settings or uncommon setups, but several can lead to running code on the server. The ones most likely to matter: CVE-2026-129289, PHP-FPM request smuggling. If nginx ( fastcgi_keep_conn on ) or Apache ( enablereuse=on ) reuses FastCGI connections, leftover bytes from a request body can be read as a second, forged request that can run code. Standard setups that close the connection aren't affected by the demonstrated attack. Three session bugs (CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714, CVE-2026-129481), including the upload-progress issue PHP warned about in October. Session upload progress is now off by default . Two PHP 8.5-only bugs in the new fatal-error backtraces. The production setting zend.exception_ignore_args=1 blocks the demonstrated attack. CVE-2026-129291 , which can turn a compromised FPM worker into root when catch_workers_output is on, as it is in the official Docker images. Check properly. Ubuntu and Debian backport fixes without changing the version, so a patched Ubuntu 24.04 still reports PHP 8.3.6. Look for the CVE in the package changelog instead: zcat /usr/share/doc/php*-common/changelog.Debian.gz | grep -m1 CVE-2026-129289 . The fixed Ubuntu 24.04 package is 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.14 . Then update and restart PHP-FPM (or Apache for mod_php). Docker users should rebuild on the new php: images. If you skipped October's release, this matters even more: the PHP2Shell bugs it fixed have been on CISA's list of exploited vulnerabilities since October 26, and this update covers them too. PHP 8.6 brings partial function application, a \Time\Duration class, clamp() , a SortDirection enum and readonly property defaults. Patch first and test 8.6 later. The exception is PHP 8.2, whose support ends on December 31, 2026. Sources PHP: PHP 8.6.0 released and November 19 security releases PHP 8 ChangeLog (8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36) PHP 8.6 release page PHP supported versions GHSA-qc49-hpvq-g2w6: PHP-FPM request smuggling (CVE-2026-129289) GHSA-658j-r8rw-q6mx: Session serializer mismatch (CVE-2026-115560) GHSA-8mjj-2r7p-4hg2: Use-after-free in magic method backtraces (CVE-2026-129474) GHSA-jm4m-qfqx-967m: PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free (CVE-2026-129291) Ubuntu changelog: php8.3 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.14 Debian security tracker: CVE-2026-129289 CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog This is the short version. The full guide, with every step and source, is on GeekSpark .

title: AI Tools Every Digital Marketer Should Learn in 2026
author: Apsana S EduStack
summary: AI Tools Every Digital Marketer Should Learn in 2026 rtificial Intelligence is changing the way digital marketers plan campaigns, create content, analyze data, and communicate with customers. In 2026, knowing how to use AI tools can give digital marketers a major advantage. However, AI is not replacing the need for marketing knowledge. Instead, marketers who know how to combine AI + creativity + strategy + data can work more efficiently and produce better results. If you are planning to build a career in digital marketing, learning the right AI tools should be part of your skill set. Why AI Is Important in Digital Marketing Digital marketing involves many repetitive and time-consuming tasks. Marketers may need to: Research keywords Create content ideas Write social media captions Analyze competitors Prepare ad copy Study campaign performance Create reports Research audiences Optimize websites Plan content calendars AI can help speed up many of these activities. The important thing is to use AI as a marketing assistant, not as a replacement for your own thinking. ChatGPT for Marketing Research and Content ChatGPT can help digital marketers with brainstorming, research, content planning, copywriting, and campaign ideas. For example, marketers can use it to generate: Blog topic ideas Social media content ideas Ad copy variations Email drafts Content calendars Customer personas Keyword research ideas Marketing strategies The quality of the result depends heavily on the instructions you provide. Learning how to write effective prompts is therefore becoming an important digital marketing skill. Canva for AI-Powered Content Creation Visual content is essential for social media marketing. Canva can help marketers create: Instagram posts Reels Carousels Presentations Advertisements Infographics Marketing banners AI-powered design features can help speed up the creative process, but marketers still need to understand branding, typography, layout, visual hierarchy, and audience preferences. AI Tools for SEO SEO is also changing with the growth of AI-powered search. Digital marketers can use AI to assist with: Keyword research Search intent analysis Content outlines Topic clustering Content optimization Competitor research SEO briefs But simply generating AI-written articles is not a complete SEO strategy. Successful SEO still requires useful content, search intent understanding, technical optimization, internal linking, authority building, and continuous performance analysis. AI for Social Media Marketing Social media marketers can use AI to speed up content planning and idea generation. For example, AI can help create: Reel ideas Caption variations Content calendars Campaign concepts Hook ideas Audience-specific content However, content should still feel authentic and relevant to the brand. The best strategy is to use AI for brainstorming and efficiency while keeping human creativity at the center. AI for Advertising AI is becoming increasingly important in digital advertising platforms. Modern advertising platforms use machine learning for areas such as audience targeting, campaign optimization, bidding, creative testing, and performance prediction. Digital marketers should therefore understand both AI-powered advertising tools and fundamental advertising principles. You still need to understand metrics such as: CTR CPC CPM Conversion Rate Cost Per Lead ROAS AI can help with optimization, but marketers need to understand what the numbers actually mean. AI for Data Analysis Digital marketing produces large amounts of data. AI can help marketers identify patterns and understand campaign performance more quickly. For example, marketers can use AI to analyze: Website traffic Campaign performance Customer behavior Conversion data Social media engagement Advertising results The goal is not simply to collect data. The goal is to turn data into marketing decisions. AI Will Not Replace Digital Marketers One common question is whether AI will replace digital marketing jobs. AI can automate many repetitive tasks, but marketing still requires human skills. A good marketer needs to understand: Audience → Problem → Strategy → Content → Campaign → Data → Optimization AI can assist with several steps in this process, but human judgment is still important. Creativity, communication, critical thinking, business understanding, and decision-making remain valuable skills. The Most Valuable Skill: Knowing How to Use AI You do not need to learn every AI tool available. Instead, focus on learning how AI can improve your existing digital marketing skills. For example: SEO + AI Use AI for research and content planning while applying proper SEO strategy. Social Media + AI Use AI for content ideas while maintaining a strong brand voice. Google Ads + AI Use automated campaign features while understanding targeting, budgets, keywords, and conversions. Content Marketing + AI Use AI to speed up content creation while adding original insights and expertise. How Beginners Can Start If you are new to digital marketing, follow a simple learning path. Step 1: Learn Digital Marketing Fundamentals Understand SEO, social media marketing, Google Ads, Meta Ads, content marketing, email marketing, and analytics. Step 2: Learn AI Tools Start with a few useful tools instead of trying everything at once. Step 3: Practise With Real Projects Create sample campaigns, blogs, social media posts, SEO reports, and advertising plans. Step 4: Build a Portfolio Document your projects and results. A portfolio can demonstrate your practical skills to potential employers or clients. Step 5: Keep Learning AI tools and digital platforms change quickly. Continuous learning is becoming an important part of a digital marketing career. Final Thoughts AI is not simply another trend in digital marketing. It is becoming part of the way marketers research, create, advertise, analyze, and optimize. The marketers who succeed in the coming years will not necessarily be those who use the most AI tools. They will be the ones who understand marketing fundamentals and know how to use AI effectively. Learn the tools. Understand the strategy. Practise with real projects. Measure your results. That is how you can prepare yourself for the future of digital marketing.

title: 3D Product Animation: How CGI Is Transforming Modern Product Marketing
author: FilmByHim
summary: In today's competitive digital marketplace, attracting customer attention has become more challenging than ever. Businesses are constantly looking for creative ways to present their products, communicate their features, and build trust with potential customers. Traditional product photography and promotional videos remain valuable, but modern technology has introduced another powerful approach: 3D product animation. Using computer-generated imagery (CGI), businesses can present their products through realistic digital models, cinematic camera movements, detailed textures, and engaging animations. These visuals allow customers to understand a product's appearance, functionality, and unique features in ways that traditional images may not always achieve. From consumer electronics and cosmetics to industrial machinery and medical equipment, 3D product animation is becoming an important tool for modern marketing and communication. Let's explore how this technology works and why businesses are increasingly incorporating it into their visual marketing strategies. 1. What Is 3D Product Animation? 3D product animation is the process of creating digital three-dimensional models of physical products and bringing them to life through animation. Artists use specialized software to build accurate product models, apply realistic materials, create lighting environments, and animate different elements. The final result can look remarkably similar to professionally filmed product footage. For example, a company launching a new smartphone can use 3D animation to showcase its design, camera system, internal components, screen features, and different colour options. Similarly, a manufacturing company can use animated sequences to demonstrate how a machine operates without physically recording every mechanical process. This makes 3D animation useful for both creative marketing and technical communication. 2. Why Brands Are Investing in CGI Product Videos Visual presentation has a major influence on how customers understand products. When customers shop online, they often depend on photographs, videos, descriptions, and product demonstrations to make purchasing decisions. 3D product animation provides additional creative flexibility by allowing brands to show details that may be difficult to capture using conventional cameras. Some important advantages include: Showcasing products from multiple angles. Demonstrating internal components and mechanisms. Highlighting product features through animation. Creating consistent visuals for different campaigns. Presenting products before physical manufacturing is complete. Producing promotional content for different digital platforms. For businesses launching new products, CGI can also reduce dependence on repeated physical photography sessions when designs or product variations change. 3. The Process Behind Professional 3D Product Animation Creating a professional 3D product animation involves several stages. Each stage contributes to the quality, accuracy, and overall appearance of the final video. 3D Modeling The process begins with creating a digital representation of the product. Artists use reference photographs, engineering drawings, CAD files, or physical samples to develop the model. The objective is to reproduce the product's dimensions, shape, proportions, and important details accurately. Texturing and Materials After modeling, artists apply materials and textures to the digital object. These materials determine how different surfaces appear under lighting. For example, glass, metal, plastic, rubber, and fabric all interact with light differently. Realistic materials are essential for producing convincing product visuals. Lighting and Camera Setup Lighting helps establish the appearance and atmosphere of a product animation. Artists create digital lighting environments and position virtual cameras to highlight important product features. A carefully planned camera movement can make even a simple product reveal look visually impressive. Animation The next stage involves adding movement. Depending on the project, artists may create rotating product views, exploded diagrams, mechanical demonstrations, liquid simulations, or cinematic product reveals. Rendering and Post-Production Rendering converts the completed digital scene into individual images or video sequences. These sequences are then edited, colour-graded, and combined with sound design, music, and other visual elements. The final video is exported according to the requirements of the intended platform. 4. Different Types of 3D Product Animation Not every business requires the same type of product video. The creative approach depends on the product, audience, and marketing objective. Here are some popular types of 3D product animation. Cinematic Product Reveal A cinematic product reveal focuses on introducing a product through dramatic lighting, creative camera movements, and detailed visual presentation. It is commonly used for product launches, advertisements, and promotional campaigns. Exploded View Animation Exploded view animation separates the different components of a product to show how they fit together. This technique is particularly useful for electronics, machinery, automotive components, and technical products. Product Demonstration Videos Product demonstration animations explain how a product works and highlight its most important features. They are useful for businesses that sell complex products or equipment. 360-Degree Product Animation A 360-degree animation allows viewers to see a product from different angles. It is useful for e-commerce websites, product presentations, and digital catalogues. CGI Advertisement CGI advertisements use digitally created visuals to develop creative promotional campaigns. They can include realistic product movements, imaginative environments, dynamic simulations, and cinematic effects. 5. How 3D Product Animation Helps E-Commerce Businesses E-commerce businesses depend heavily on visual content because customers cannot physically inspect products before purchasing them. Product images and videos help bridge this gap by providing additional information. A well-designed 3D product animation can demonstrate product dimensions, materials, functionality, and design details. For example, a furniture brand can showcase how a modular sofa changes configuration. An electronics company can demonstrate the internal structure of a device. A cosmetics brand can present the texture and packaging of a product through realistic CGI. 3D animation can also help businesses create visual assets for: Online product listings. Website landing pages. Social media campaigns. Digital advertisements. Product launch presentations. Promotional videos. The key is to ensure that the animation accurately represents the real product rather than creating misleading expectations. 6. The Role of CGI in Social Media Advertising Social media platforms have changed how brands communicate with customers. Short videos, engaging visuals, and creative advertisements are now important parts of digital marketing strategies. CGI makes it possible to create unusual product demonstrations and visually interesting scenes that may be difficult to produce through traditional filming. For example, a beverage brand can create a digital environment where ingredients move around the product. A technology company can showcase a device through detailed internal animations. A skincare brand can use realistic liquid simulations to highlight product textures. Different versions of the same animation can also be adapted for vertical, square, and horizontal formats. This allows brands to maintain a consistent visual identity across different platforms. 7. Important Software Used in 3D Animation Professional 3D artists use different software applications depending on the requirements of a project. Some widely used tools include: Blender: A versatile application for 3D modeling, texturing, animation, rendering, and visual effects. Unreal Engine: Used for real-time rendering, interactive experiences, and high-quality digital environments. Houdini: Particularly useful for procedural workflows, simulations, particles, and complex visual effects. SketchUp: Commonly used for architectural modeling, spatial visualization, and design presentations. Each application offers different capabilities, and professional artists often combine multiple tools to achieve the desired result. 8. How to Choose a Professional 3D Animation Studio Selecting the right animation studio is an important step for businesses planning to invest in CGI. A professional studio should understand both the technical requirements and the marketing objectives of a project. Before choosing a service provider, consider the following factors: Portfolio Quality: Review previous projects to understand the studio's modeling, animation, lighting, and rendering capabilities. Technical Accuracy: For industrial and technical products, accurate dimensions and mechanical details are essential. Creative Approach: The studio should be able to develop a visual concept that communicates your product's unique value. Communication: Clear communication helps ensure that the final animation matches the original brief. Revision Process: Discuss feedback, revisions, project milestones, and delivery expectations before starting. Final Deliverables: Confirm the required video resolution, aspect ratios, formats, and usage requirements. A good creative partnership can make the production process smoother and more effective. 9. Industrial and Technical Applications of 3D Animation 3D animation is not limited to consumer products and advertisements. Manufacturing and engineering companies also use it to communicate complex technical information. Industrial animation can demonstrate how machines operate, explain manufacturing processes, and visualize internal mechanical components. For example, an animated industrial production line can show how raw materials move through different manufacturing stages. Similarly, a machine animation can reveal the movement of gears, motors, and other internal components. These visual explanations can be useful for: Employee training. Technical presentations. Engineering demonstrations. Industrial marketing. Product documentation. Safety education. By converting complicated information into visual sequences, 3D animation can make technical communication easier to understand. 10. FilmByHim: Creating Professional 3D Product Animations and CGI Visuals Choosing the right creative partner is important when developing high-quality product animations. FilmByHim offers creative solutions in 3D product animation, CGI, visual effects, motion graphics, and professional post-production. The studio focuses on transforming product concepts and technical information into engaging visual content. Its 3D product animation services cover areas such as: Photorealistic 3D product modeling. Product demonstration videos. Cinematic product launch animations. Amazon listing animations. Exploded view animations. CGI promotional advertisements. Product visualization. Businesses interested in professional CGI and product visualization can explore FilmByHim's 3D Product Animation Services to learn more about its creative capabilities. For projects involving complex visual effects and digital compositing, the studio also offers VFX and CGI Services You can visit the FilmByHim official website to explore its broader range of post-production and creative services. 11. The Future of 3D Product Animation The future of 3D product animation is closely connected to developments in artificial intelligence, real-time rendering, virtual reality, and interactive digital experiences. Businesses are exploring new ways to allow customers to interact with products before making purchasing decisions. Some emerging applications include: Interactive 3D Models: Customers can rotate, zoom, and explore digital product models. Augmented Reality: Digital products can be placed into real-world environments through compatible devices. Real-Time Rendering: Artists can make visual adjustments and preview scenes more quickly. AI-Assisted Workflows: Artificial intelligence can support certain repetitive production tasks and creative processes. Virtual Product Experiences: Brands can create immersive environments where customers explore products digitally. These technologies are creating new opportunities for product marketing, education, and digital commerce. However, creative direction, accurate modeling, and professional visual quality will remain essential. Conclusion 3D product animation has become an important part of modern visual communication. It allows businesses to present products creatively, explain complicated features, and develop engaging promotional content. From realistic product demonstrations to cinematic CGI advertisements, digital animation offers flexibility that traditional photography alone may not provide. As online competition continues to grow, businesses need visual content that communicates clearly and captures attention. Investing in professional 3D modeling, animation, rendering, and post-production can help brands develop more effective visual presentations. Ultimately, great product animation is not just about creating beautiful digital images. It is about presenting a product's story in a way that people can understand, appreciate, and remember. https://www.filmbyhim.com/

title: The maintainer answered my PR in 13 minutes. I saw it two days later.
author: Zhuojun Li
summary: lot-map 0.13.0 came out on Nov 21 with an option I asked for. commandStations puts a shell command on a station of your choice. I set agent-dispatch=agents , so when a Claude Code session hands an order to another model, the map lights Agents instead of Shell. The previous post was about the half lot-map will never show: the queue outside the session. This is the half it can. The timeline All times UTC. Nov 18: I opened issue #103 . The maintainer said yes the same day and told me where the command had to be found: behind sudo , env , bash -c and docker exec , not only as the first word of the line. Nov 19, 01:29: PR #111 . Nov 19, 01:42: his review. One change, then he would merge. Nov 21, 03:58: my reply. Nov 21, 04:13: merged. 04:32: released. The 50 hours in the middle are mine. I missed the notification. In those two days five other PRs changed the same lines of classify.ts , so I had to rebase before I could answer. What he asked for My version said a command you place stays where you put it. That put agent-dispatch status && curl https://example.com/x on Agents, and the curl went unseen. His rule has two parts. A placed command keeps its station whatever its own name says, so gh=agents stays on Agents. Another command on the same line that reaches the network takes the whole line to Network. In his words, "a curl should not hide behind its neighbour." He was right. Network is the station you watch to see whether something left the machine. I had asked for a convenience and nearly traded that away. The change was two commits and four new tests, 202 passing where next had 198. If you run lot-map, update anyway 0.13.0 also fixes a label that could show a secret. A PowerShell line like $token = "ghp_…" with no description was labelled with the value. The release notes list it first. To use the new option: /plugin configure lot-map , then commandStations , then one entry per command, written command=station . The stations are files, shell, web, browser, agents, skills and you. I ran nine of my real command lines through the 0.13.0 classifier. The six that call the dispatcher land on Agents, and the one chained to curl lands on Network. After a restart of VS Code, Agents lit up in a session that was preparing work orders. I have not yet watched it through a day of orders. Zhuojun Li
